content: The document is a systematic overview of systematic reviews on comprehensive school health services (SHS), developed in partnership with the World Health Organization (WHO). It outlines the methodology and findings of the reviews, focusing on interventions aimed at improving the health of school-aged children and adolescents. 1. Collaboration and Purpose: This work was conducted in collaboration with the WHO and is part of the WHO guideline on school health services. It aims to provide a systematic overview of existing systematic reviews on comprehensive SHS, focusing on their methodology and selected findings. 2. Licensing and Usage: The publication is licensed under Creative Commons, allowing non-commercial use, redistribution, and adaptation, provided proper citation is given. The WHO logo cannot be used, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or equivalent terms. Translations must include a disclaimer stating that the WHO is not responsible for the content or accuracy of the translation. 3. Methodology: The overview followed the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines. A protocol was developed in advance, detailing objectives, search strategies, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and quality appraisal methods. Systematic searches were conducted in databases such as PubMed, Web of Science, ERIC, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane Library. 4. Eligibility Criteria: Systematic reviews were included if at least 50% of the studies met the following criteria: Participants were children (ages 5–9) or adolescents (ages 10–19) enrolled in schools. Interventions were school-based or school-linked, involved a health provider, and had any duration or follow-up length. Effectiveness was compared to no intervention, alternative interventions, or active/waitlist controls. Interventions aimed to improve health outcomes. Study designs included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled studies (NCSs), or other non-randomized intervention studies. Reviews had to include the term systematic review in the title or abstract, outline inclusion criteria in the methods section, be published in peer-reviewed journals before June 15, 2018, and be in English. 5. Study Selection and Data Collection: Citations were uploaded to Covidence software, and duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, resolving conflicts through discussion. Full texts of potentially eligible articles were reviewed, and reasons for exclusion were documented. Data extraction was performed using a standardized form, with independent verification for 15% of the reviews. There was a 92% agreement between reviewers. 6. Findings: The strongest evidence supported the implementation of anxiety prevention programs, asthma education, and vision screening with free spectacles. However, no review evaluated the effectiveness of a comprehensive SHS intervention addressing multiple health areas. 7. Risk of Bias: Risk of bias across systematic reviews was assessed using a four-item checklist, including overlap, confidence ratings, publication date, and scope alignment. The heterogeneity of the included reviews precluded meta-analysis. 8. Acknowledgments and Contributors: The guideline was developed by a team of experts, including Mary Louisa Plummer, David A. Ross, and Nandi Siegfried, among others. The steering group and external review group included representatives from WHO, academic institutions, and other organizations. 9. Funding: Financial support was provided by the UK Department for International Development, the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, and the United States Agency for International Development. 10. Glossary and Abbreviations: The document includes a glossary of terms and abbreviations used throughout, such as BMI (body mass index), RCT (randomized controlled trial), and SMD (standardized mean difference). This publication is part of the WHO guideline on school health services and is made publicly available for transparency and informational purposes, in line with the WHO handbook for guideline development.
